title: AWS Accounts, Free Tier, and Billing

questions.prompt: Which statement about the root user is correct?

options.text: It has complete, unrestricted access and should be protected with MFA and rarely used
It has only read-only access to the account
It is the best identity to use for daily work

questions.explanation: The root user has full, unrestricted access. Because it can't be scoped down, you enable MFA, avoid daily use, and don't give it access keys.

questions.prompt: Which are recommended steps for a brand-new AWS account? Select all that apply.

options.text: Enable MFA on the root user
Create a separate identity for daily work
Create access keys for the root user for convenience

questions.explanation: Enable MFA, use a separate daily identity, and set a budget. You should NOT create root access keys — that's explicitly discouraged.

questions.prompt: Does 'Free Tier' mean everything on AWS is free?

options.text: Yes, all services are free for the first 12 months
No — only specific services up to specific limits are free; overages and non-Free-Tier services cost money

questions.explanation: The Free Tier covers specific services up to specific limits (12-month, always-free, and trial offers). Exceeding a limit or using another service incurs charges.

questions.prompt: To be alerted when your spending is forecast to exceed a threshold, you create an AWS ____.
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets lets you set a cost or usage threshold and receive an email alert when you're forecast to exceed it.

questions.prompt: Match each billing tool to what it does.

pairs.right: Alerts you when spend/usage crosses a threshold
Charts and breaks down past and forecast spending
Label resources so spend can be grouped by project

questions.explanation: Budgets alert, Cost Explorer visualizes, tags group spend by label, and Organizations consolidates billing across accounts.

questions.prompt: What uniquely identifies an AWS account?

options.text: The Region it was created in
The name of the first EC2 instance

questions.explanation: Every AWS account has a unique 12-digit account ID (for example, 123456789012); all its resources and charges roll up to that account.
